prose.xlsx_fail_note: not one of the 4 large tables here fits in one: they run from 1.200.000 to 4.208.256 rows.
prose.pq_smallest_where: 5 of the 8 corpus and scale combinations
prose.feather_write_note: Writing the 393.6 MB power flow table took 567 ms against 2.26 s for Parquet zstd, and reading it back took 213 ms.
prose.columnar_note: On the wide table the three requested columns are 3 of 41, about 7% of the data. Parquet zstd read them in 63 ms against 572 ms for the whole file, 9.1 times faster; DuckDB table did best at 14 times. CSV read them in 5.78 s against 8.21 s, a saving of 30%, because usecols still has to parse every byte of every row to find the commas. That gap, 92 times between CSV and Parquet on the same question, is the single largest effect measured on this page.
prose.pareto_note: Nothing on the frontier is a surprise once you see it: Parquet gzip, Parquet zstd, Parquet snappy, Feather zstd, Feather lz4, Feather (uncompressed). Everything else is dominated, which includes every text format. CSV is 2.6 times the size of Parquet zstd and 14 times slower to read: it loses on both axes at once, so there is no trade to discuss. Where the frontier is genuinely a trade is between uncompressed Feather at 393.7 MB and 213 ms and Parquet zstd at 239.8 MB and 572 ms: 61% of the bytes for 2.7 times the read time.
prose.scale_note: At 100.000 rows the whole question is close to academic: the difference between CSV and Parquet on the wide table is 703 ms against 85 ms, and nobody notices either. At 1.200.000 rows it is 8.21 s against 572 ms, and it is the difference between an interactive script and a coffee break. The ranking barely moves with size; what moves is whether the ranking matters.
prose.fidelity_note: 7 of 13 formats returned the frame unchanged: Feather (uncompressed), Feather lz4, Feather zstd, Parquet (uncompressed), Parquet snappy, Parquet zstd, Parquet gzip. The text formats lost between 5 and 5 of the six properties, and lost them silently: nothing raises, nothing warns, the frame simply comes back different. CSV lost 5. CSV .gz lost 5. JSON lost 5.
prose.tz_note: CSV writes an ISO string with an offset, which looks like it survived. It has not: the offset is a number, not a zone, so the reader has to be told to parse it and to localize the result. Miss that and pandas 3 gives you a naive column that silently compares false against every aware timestamp in your code. Measured here: the instant survives but the zone does not: local_ts datetime64[us, Europe/Amsterdam] to str. The Europe/Amsterdam column crosses the CEST transition, so its offsets are mixed, and pandas will not parse a mixed-offset column back into one datetime column at all: it stays a string unless you handle it yourself.. Excel is worse: xlsxwriter refuses a tz-aware datetime outright, so the zone has to be stripped before writing and there is nothing in the file that records which zone it was. Parquet, Feather and DuckDB all store the zone with the value.
prose.null_note: A nullable Int32 with four missing values comes back from CSV as float64: pandas has no way to know you wanted an integer, and NaN forces the column to float. Station numbers and unit ids become 260.0. Measured: gaps kept, but the nullable integer became float64 and the nullable bool object. The nullable boolean has the same problem, becoming object or float depending on the reader. Parquet and Feather carry a validity bitmap next to the values, so the distinction between zero and missing is part of the file.
prose.cat_note: An ordered categorical of bidding zones comes back from every text format as plain strings: both the dictionary and the ordering are gone, and any code that sorted on the category order now sorts alphabetically. Arrow stores it as a dictionary-encoded column, which is why Feather and Parquet keep it, and why the categorical is also where they get much of their compression on the register table.
prose.mmap_note: Mapping the 393.7 MB Arrow IPC file took 2.0 ms and grew the process by 3.7 MB: nothing was read, the kernel just wired the file into the address space. Taking a numpy view of one column stayed at 24.7 MB. Reading the same file into pandas cost 362 ms and 398.5 MB, and converting the mapped table to pandas costs the same 792.0 MB, because that is the copy. So the intuition is right and the condition is exact: you get RAM-on-disc as long as you stay in Arrow. Compressing the Feather file removes the property entirely, 398.1 MB for the same map, since compressed buffers have to be decoded into memory that the file does not back. Parquet is never mappable in this sense: it is an encoded format, and pd.read_parquet cost 451 ms and 831.1 MB.
prose.cold_note: Cold, uncompressed Feather reads in 580 ms against 213 ms warm: the 393.7 MB has to come off the disk and nothing can hide that. Parquet zstd goes from 572 ms to 760 ms for 239.8 MB. The cold penalty is largest for Feather (uncompressed) at 2.7 times. The practical reading: the smaller compressed formats lose least when the cache is cold, so if your files live on a share rather than a local SSD, weight size higher than these warm numbers suggest. CSV stays slowest either way, because parsing dominates.
prose.engine_note: Changing engine on a CSV is worth something: DuckDB read the 4.208.256 row price CSV in 1.24 s where pandas took 10.2 s, 8.2 times faster, because it parses in parallel. Changing format is worth an order of magnitude more: the same data as Parquet zstd read in 106 ms in pandas, 96 times faster than the CSV it replaced. If you only change one thing, change the format. On Parquet the three engines land within a factor of 6.7 of each other, because at that point almost nothing is left to parse.
prose.claim_base: CSV as the base is right, and it is the right thing to hand to a person. The improvement is in the other direction. JSON was 2.1 times the size of the same data as CSV (319.9 MB against 151.5 MB) and 0.9 times the read time, and it cannot project columns at all. Excel is slower still and cannot hold the data: none of the four large tables fits in a worksheet. Both are worse than CSV for this workload, not better. The formats that improve on CSV are the ones further down the list: Feather and Parquet.
prose.claim_feather: Correct, and the mechanism is exactly the one implied. Uncompressed Arrow IPC is the in-memory layout written straight to disk, so it wrote the 41 column power flow table in 567 ms and read it back in 213 ms, the fastest round trip measured. Memory-mapped it is literally RAM on disc: 393.7 MB mapped in 2.0 ms with the process growing by 3.7 MB. Two conditions you have to know: compress the file and the property is gone, and convert to pandas and you have paid for the copy anyway. The cost is size: at 393.7 MB it is 1.6 times the Parquet file.
prose.claim_parquet: Correct on all three counts, and it is the right default. On the wide table it was 239.8 MB against 619.1 MB for CSV and 393.7 MB for uncompressed Feather; it read whole in 572 ms; and the columnar claim is the one that pays best, three of 41 columns in 63 ms, 9.1 times faster than the full read. The one sharpening: zstd rather than the snappy default. It was 5% smaller than snappy here for a read time within 13%, and gzip buys a little more size for a much slower write (14.7 s against 2.26 s).
prose.claim_duckdb: DuckDB belongs on the list but not in the same column as the others: it is a query engine that happens to have a storage format, not a file format that happens to be queryable. Two consequences. First, you do not have to import anything: pointed straight at the Parquet file it answered the filtered query in 111 ms, against 275 ms for pyarrow's own pushdown on the same file, and no copy of the data exists. Second, when you do import, you get things no file format offers: indexes, joins across tables, updates in place, and queries larger than memory. Its own file was 258.0 MB against 239.8 MB for Parquet, and reading a whole table out of it into pandas cost 1.99 s against 572 ms, so as a plain container it is not the best. Use it for the query, keep Parquet for the file.
prose.claim_csv_fidelity: This is the finding worth taking away. Round-tripped through CSV, the test frame lost 5 of its 6 properties, silently: index partial, came back as an ordinary column: you have to know to set it again, and to re-localize it first; dtype lost, 6 of 7 changed (local_ts: datetime64[us, Europe/Amsterdam] to str, zone: category to str, load_mw_f32: float32 to float64); tz partial, the instant survives but the zone does not: local_ts datetime64[us, Europe/Amsterdam] to str. The Europe/Amsterdam column crosses the CEST transition, so its offsets are mixed, and pandas will not parse a mixed-offset column back into one datetime column at all: it stays a string unless you handle it yourself.; null partial, gaps kept, but the nullable integer became float64 and the nullable bool object; categorical lost, returned as str: the dictionary and the ordering are gone. For grid timeseries this is not a performance question, it is a correctness one. A tz-aware UTC column that comes back naive compares false against every aware timestamp in your code without raising, and a nullable integer that comes back as float turns station 260 into 260.0 and a missing reading into NaN, which is now indistinguishable from a genuine zero after one arithmetic operation. None of this announces itself.
prose.claim_excel: Excel is a deliverable, not a storage format, and the row limit settles it before any other argument is needed. A worksheet holds 1.048.576 rows, and not one of the 4 large tables measured here fits: they run from 1.200.000 to 4.208.256 rows. Even where it fits, writing the 100.000 row wide table took 36.8 s against 297 ms for Parquet, reading it back took 20.7 s, and the file was 2 times larger. It also drops the timezone from every timestamp on the way in. Generate it last, from the real file, for a human who is going to look at it.
prose.method_corpus: Four generated corpora shaped like the files this work actually produces, each at two scales, written and re-read by 13 formats. 97 format and corpus combinations completed, 7 were impossible and are reported as impossible rather than omitted. Every timing is the median of repeated runs, 7 at the small scale and 4 at the large one, with expensive combinations stopping early against a 40 second budget; the number of repeats actually taken is recorded per cell in the raw data.
prose.method_noise: These ran on a shared container with other heavy jobs on the same four cores, so absolute milliseconds here are not a property of the formats. Medians of several repeats absorb some of that and the ratios between formats measured back to back are sound, but treat a difference under about 20% as noise, and do not compare a number on this page against a number from your own laptop.
prose.method_gaps: No lazy or streaming reads: everything is materialised into a pandas DataFrame, so polars scan_parquet and DuckDB's out-of-core execution are not represented and both would look better if they were. No partitioned Parquet datasets, which change the filtered-query numbers substantially when the predicate matches the partition key. No Arrow Flight, no ORC, no HDF5 or NetCDF, which matter for weather in particular. Nothing here is measured over a network filesystem.
